source.title: Simplicity Bias Leads to Amplified Performance Disparities

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the full paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies group difficulty and performance disparities on naturally labeled tasks. It does not test random-label fitting, unstructured inputs, label-noise degradation, regularization effects on random-label fitting, or the order in which real and noisy labels are learned.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training dynamics on naturally labeled groups: an easier group is learned faster, and both groups eventually reach perfect training accuracy. These results do not test any listed claim version. Background references to prior work on memorization are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures learning speed and performance disparities between naturally labeled groups. It never compares real labels with noisy or random labels, corrupts inputs, or tests random-label fitting. Its simplicity-bias results therefore do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The broader conclusion is that difficulty depends jointly on model and data, and some models amplify group test-performance disparities even with balanced data. Amplification varies with architecture, scale, training time, and regularization; targeted additional data or oversampling may reduce it.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates group difficulty and performance disparity rather than random-label memorization.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that group learning dynamics and disparity vary with dataset, model architecture, model width, training time, and regularization strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-18 learns simpler naturally labeled groups faster than more complex groups, while both eventually reach perfect training accuracy on CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and EMNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning speed differs between naturally labeled groups of different model-perceived difficulty, even when both groups can be fit perfectly.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Technology (FAccT ’23)
record.problems: The relevant training-accuracy statements are qualitative; precise values are shown in figures. The experiments concern naturally labeled groups and do not address random-label memorization.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on the listed claim versions were reported. Test-accuracy and disparity findings were omitted because they concern group performance disparities rather than the specified random-label behaviors.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for random and true labels, and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across a label-corruption sweep.
Regularization effects on random-label fitting and generalization after removing regularization. The weight-decay experiment measures disparity amplification instead.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: The row states describe whether these measures establish the listed claim versions; cannot_determine does not dispute the reported natural-label training results. Citations to memorization and simplicity-bias research provide background rather than additional tests.

versions.untested_parts: Random labeling, chance test error, and whether fitting requires changes to architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time for fitting random versus true labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across a sweep from clean labels to completely random labels.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The study compares learning speed across naturally labeled groups but does not test whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a combined synthetic binary task built from two CIFAR-100 class pairs; reports training accuracy by group.

conditions.value: simple group: flowers vs. aquatic mammals

rows.value: Both groups reach perfect train accuracy eventually.
rows.uncertainty: Shading is standard error over 10 runs with different train/test splits.
rows.note: The text states both groups eventually reach perfect training accuracy; no numeric accuracy value is given.
rows.check: The reported perfect training accuracy is supported, but concerns natural CIFAR-100 labels and cannot establish any listed version.

rows.operation_detail: Trained on a combined synthetic binary task built from two CIFAR-100 class pairs; reports training accuracy by group.

conditions.value: complex group: medium mammals vs. carnivores

rows.uncertainty: Shading is standard error over 10 runs with different train/test splits.

rows.check: Slower learning and eventual perfect training accuracy concern a harder naturally labeled group, not noisy or random labels.
